lines: Fine weather for it. The crows have taken to following people instead of the plough.
They stop at the gate. I have not asked them why.
You'll want to be off the fields before the last lamp. Not that anything happens. It's just what we do.
There's water in the pump if you want it. Don't drink from the well. It has tasted of pennies since March.
We lock the door at nine. You would be welcome, but we lock it at nine.
I've stood at this gate most days for forty years. The road used to go somewhere else.
The lamps are lit at dusk and counted at ten. Somebody has to count them.

country_woman.speaker: A Woman in a Brown Coat

lines: Walking to Castle? Keep to the road. The fields are fine. It's what is in them.
Go on, get indoors somewhere. I'm only waiting for my husband. He is usually back by now.
I cut on this side of the wood. Nobody cuts the other side, and it doesn't grow.
I leave the axe in the stump overnight. In the morning it is never quite where I left it.
The water is higher than it was. It doesn't rain any more than it used to. It just is higher.
If you hear somebody calling from the water, it's the herons. Mostly.
Rooms by the week. Nobody has taken one since the spring, but the beds are made every morning.
Doors shut at nine. If anyone knocks after that, it isn't us they want.

country_man.speaker: A Man in a Grey Coat

lines: I'm waiting for the carrier. He comes on Tuesdays.
It isn't Tuesday. I know it isn't. I like to be early.
You knock. Somebody inside stops what they were doing, and waits for you to go.
Nobody answers. There is a clean cup on the step, upside down, the way you leave one for somebody.
The door is locked. Through the window: a table laid for four, and three chairs.
A voice says, not unkindly, that they don't open to people off the road.
The light inside goes out while you are still knocking.
The door gives an inch and stops. Something heavy has been pushed against it from the inside.
The doors are barred on the outside. A card is pinned to them: PLEASE DON'T LOOK IN THE BARN. THANK YOU.
Padlocked. The padlock is new and the shed is not.
THE HALFWAY HOUSE. ROOMS. TEAS. Halfway between what, the sign does not say.
A bucket on a chain. The water at the bottom is further down than the chain is long.
A candle in a box on a post. It was lit today, and nobody has passed you on this road.
EGGS. HONESTY BOX. The box is full of buttons.
Blankets, a tin plate, and a pair of good boots with nobody's feet in them.
The earth at the mouth is worn smooth. Whatever lives here has been coming and going for years.
The hive is quiet. You are meant to tell the bees when somebody dies. Nobody has told these anything for a while.
The handle is warm, as if somebody put it down a moment ago.
The name has worn away. The flowers on it are fresh.
The hen watches the road the whole time you stand there. Not you: the road.
The sheep all face the same way. It is not the way the wind is blowing.
It does not run until you are two steps away. Then it runs, and stops, and waits for you again.
